statement: A property-carrying CMV driver may drive a total of 11 hours inside the 14-hour period that starts after 10 consecutive hours off duty. Applies to interstate CMVs of 10,001 lb GVWR or more (49 CFR 390.5); a cargo van under 10,001 lb is not a CMV and is not bound.

No driving after the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time inside the window does not extend it. Non-CDL short-haul drivers under 395.1(e)(2) are exempt from this paragraph and instead may not drive after the 14th hour on 5 days, or after the 16th hour on 2 days, of any 7 consecutive days.

Driving is not permitted once 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status (off duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving all count). Drivers who qualify for either short-haul exception in 395.1(e)(1) or (e)(2) are exempt.

No driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; 70 hours in 8 consecutive days if it does. Either period may be restarted by 34 or more consecutive hours off duty. Value is the 60/7 limit because most small local carriers do not run 7 days; use 70 (8 days) when the scenario runs every day.

A driver is exempt from logbook/ELD requirements (395.8, 395.11) if they operate within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location, return there and are released within 14 consecutive hours, and (property-carrying) have at least 10 consecutive hours off duty between each 14 hours on duty; the carrier keeps time records (report time, hours on duty, release time) for 6 months. These drivers are also exempt from the 30-minute break.

A CDL is required for a single vehicle with GVWR/GVW of 26,001 lb or more (Group B, heavy straight vehicle), or a combination with GCWR/GCW of 26,001 lb or more towing a unit over 10,000 lb (Group A). The vehicle's GVWR rating plate decides it, not its length.

A vehicle used in interstate commerce with GVWR/GCWR or GVW/GCW of 10,001 lb or more is a commercial motor vehicle under the FMCSRs; each motor carrier (private, exempt for-hire and for-hire) subject to the subchapter must register through the Unified Registration System (Form MCSA-1) to be identified for safety oversight and, if for-hire, obtain operating authority. Intrastate-only carriers are governed by state rules not captured here.
cfr: 49 CFR 390.5 (definition of commercial motor vehicle); 49 CFR 390.201(b)

statement: Maximum gross vehicle weight on the Interstate System is 80,000 lb, unless the bridge formula dictates lower. Note: this federal limit lives in Title 23 (FHWA), not Title 49.

Maximum gross weight on any one axle is 20,000 lb; on tandem axles 34,000 lb; two or more consecutive axles are further bounded by the Bridge Gross Weight Formula. Value is the single-axle limit. Title 23 (FHWA), not Title 49.

A CMV driver must be medically certified as physically qualified and carry the original or a copy of a current medical examiner's certificate when on duty; a driver not examined and certified within the preceding 24 months may not drive (shorter intervals apply when the examiner sets one).

A carrier may have a driver keep a paper record of duty status instead of an ELD if the driver needs a record of duty status on not more than 8 days in any 30-day period, is in certain driveaway-towaway operations, or drives a vehicle manufactured before model year 2000. Short-haul drivers under 395.1(e) are exempt from 395.8 entirely.

Before a driver subject to Part 382 testing (CDL holders) performs any safety-sensitive function, the employer must run a pre-employment full query of the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, and must query every such driver at least once per year (a limited query with driver consent satisfies the annual requirement).
